newsitem.title: USA: Stocks rise, but bonds weak.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rise, but bonds weak.

text.p: Stocks managed modest gains Friday after the government said unemployment fell to a 23-year low in April but a weak bond market prevented a broader rally.

Just before 1:30 p.m., the Dow Jones industrial average was up 32.91 points at 7,009.39, while in the broader market advancing issues led declines by nearly 3-1 on active volume of about 279 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp., said there appeared to be little exuberance in the market Friday, "irrational or otherwise."
He said he was disappointed by the bond market's weak response to what he viewed as a favourable jobs report.
"The good news is that the economy is slowing even though there is a tightness in labour markets," Johnson said.

The Labour Department said the unemployment rate fell to 4.9 percent last month -- its lowest level since December 1973 -- from 5.2 percent in March, even though the economy created a modest 142,000 jobs.

The jobs report, the government's first look at the economy in April, followed a report on Wednesday that the economy grew at a 5.6 percent rate in the first quarter, the strongest performance in nine years.
After rallying earlier in the week on economic news and the prospect for a balanced budget deal, bond prices edged lower Friday, which in turn held back the stock market.
The 30-year Treasury bond lost 5/32, or $1.56 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.93 percent from 6.92 percent on Thursday. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Some traders and investors admitted the April jobs report was difficult to read. While the unemployment rate sank -- pointing to tightness in the labour market that could be inflationary -- job growth came in well below Wall Street forecasts for 211,000 jobs outside the farm sector.
The report, while painting a picture of healthy job growth with little wage-driven inflation, could still fuel the case for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again.

The central bank raised short-term rates a quarter point at its last meeting in March -- the first increase in 26 months -- and when Fed policy-makers meet on May 20 the jobs report will weigh heavily in their thinking, economists said.
"This number still leaves open the door" for a rate hike, said Astrid Adolfson, economist at MCM Moneywatch Inc., referring to the unemployment rate in the jobs report.

"A lot of economists and bond traders were confused by the numbers. There was something there for both the bulls and bears of the bond market," said Anthony O'Bryan, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons.
"But the stock market has given the report a vote of confidence."
Johnson also said the stock market was seeing a shift of interest into smaller stocks and out of the big blue-chip issues that have led the bull market so far.

The Nasdaq Composite Index jumped 20.97 points, or 1.65 percent, to 1,291.47 and the Russell 2000 index of smaller company shares rose 4.64 to 350.30 -- both bigger percentage gains than the 30-share Dow.
The American Stock Exchange index added 2.31 points to 560.81.
